text: He ____ in Lahore since 2015.
explanation: An action that began at a stated point in the past and still continues takes the present perfect continuous with 'since'.

text: She ____ her homework before the guests arrived.
explanation: The earlier of two past actions is expressed by the past perfect, so 'had finished' precedes 'arrived'.

text: Water ____ at 100 degrees Celsius.
explanation: Universal truths and scientific facts are stated in the simple present tense.

text: By the time you arrive, I ____ the report.
explanation: An action to be finished before a future point takes the future perfect tense.

text: Look! The baby ____ in the next room.
explanation: 'Look!' signals an action happening at the moment of speaking, which requires the present continuous.

text: I ____ him at the conference yesterday.
explanation: A finished action with a definite past time marker such as 'yesterday' takes the simple past.

text: They ____ for two hours when the coach arrived.
explanation: An activity continuing over a period up to a past moment takes the past perfect continuous.

text: The train ____ before we reached the station.
explanation: The action completed earlier than another past action ('reached') is put in the past perfect.

text: If it rains tomorrow, we ____ the match.
explanation: In a first conditional the if-clause is in the present simple and the main clause takes 'will' + base verb.

text: He said that he ____ tired.
explanation: When the reporting verb is in the past, the reported verb is back-shifted to the past tense.

text: I ____ my breakfast when the phone rang.
explanation: The longer background action is in the past continuous and the sudden action in the simple past.

text: He ____ smoke, but he gave it up last year.
explanation: 'Used to' + base verb expresses a discontinued past habit; 'is/was used to' means accustomed to.

text: We ____ each other since childhood.
explanation: 'Know' is a stative verb, so a state continuing from the past to now takes the present perfect simple.

text: Hardly had he entered the room when the lights ____ out.
explanation: In the 'hardly had ... when' pattern the second clause takes the simple past.

text: I have never ____ such a beautiful sunset.
explanation: After 'have/has' the third form of the verb (past participle) is used, which is 'seen'.

text: The work ____ by the students yesterday.
explanation: A past action seen from the point of view of the object takes the past simple passive 'was done'.

text: English ____ all over the world.
explanation: The subject receives the action, so the present simple passive 'is spoken' is required.

text: I wish I ____ rich enough to buy that house.
explanation: After 'I wish' an unreal present situation takes the past subjunctive 'were' for all persons.

text: He will call you as soon as he ____ home.
explanation: After time conjunctions such as 'as soon as', future meaning is expressed by the present simple, not 'will'.

text: She ____ to Karachi three times.
explanation: Experience up to the present, with no stated past time, takes the present perfect 'has been'.

text: This time tomorrow I ____ over the Atlantic.
explanation: An action in progress at a stated future moment takes the future continuous tense.

text: He is not here yet; he must ____ the train.
explanation: A confident deduction about the past is expressed by 'must have' + past participle.

text: She avoided ____ the question put by the reporter.
explanation: The verb 'avoid' is always followed by a gerund, never by an infinitive.

text: I look forward to ____ from you soon.
explanation: In 'look forward to' the word 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the gerund.

text: It is high time we ____ home.
explanation: 'It is high time' is followed by the past subjunctive form of the verb although the sense is present.

text: If he had studied harder, he ____ the examination.
explanation: In the third conditional the main clause takes 'would have' + past participle.

text: He is ____ honest man and everyone trusts him.
explanation: The 'h' in 'honest' is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound and takes 'an'.

text: ____ Nile is the longest river in Africa.
explanation: Names of rivers always take the definite article 'the'.

text: She plays ____ piano very well.
explanation: Names of musical instruments take the definite article when we speak of playing them.

text: He is ____ university student in his final year.
explanation: 'University' begins with the consonant sound /ju:/, so it takes 'a' and not 'an'.

text: I bought ____ umbrella from the market yesterday.
explanation: 'Umbrella' begins with a vowel sound, so the indefinite article 'an' is used.

text: ____ moon revolves round the earth.
explanation: Unique objects in nature such as the moon, the sun and the sky take the definite article.

text: Children in Pakistan go to ____ school at the age of five.
explanation: Institutions such as school, college and hospital take no article when referred to for their primary purpose.

text: He is ____ best student in the class.
explanation: Superlative adjectives are preceded by the definite article 'the'.

text: There is ____ hospital at the end of this road.
explanation: A singular countable noun mentioned for the first time and beginning with a consonant sound takes 'a'.

text: ____ rich should help the poor.
explanation: An adjective used as a plural common noun for a whole class takes the definite article.

text: She is ____ M.A. in Economics.
explanation: The letter M is pronounced /em/, a vowel sound, so the abbreviation takes 'an'.

text: He gave me ____ one-rupee coin as a souvenir.
explanation: 'One' begins with the consonant sound /w/, so it takes 'a' in spite of the vowel letter.

text: ____ Himalayas separate the subcontinent from Tibet.
explanation: Names of mountain ranges, unlike single peaks, take the definite article.

text: ____ Holy Quran is a complete code of life.
explanation: Names of sacred books take the definite article 'the'.

text: She has been teaching in this college ____ 2010.
explanation: 'Since' is used with a point of time, while 'for' is used with a length of time.

text: He is good ____ mathematics.
explanation: The adjective 'good' takes the preposition 'at' when it refers to skill in a subject or activity.

text: She is married ____ a doctor.
explanation: The standard collocation is 'married to' a person.

text: The clerk was accused ____ theft.
explanation: One is accused of an offence, although one is charged with it.

text: Distribute these sweets ____ the two boys.
explanation: 'Between' is used for two persons or things and 'among' for more than two.

text: The book is divided ____ five chapters.
explanation: 'Divide into' shows the parts something is separated in to.

text: He congratulated me ____ my success.
explanation: The verb 'congratulate' takes the preposition 'on' before the occasion.

text: She insisted ____ going alone.
explanation: 'Insist' is followed by 'on' and then a gerund.

text: I have no objection ____ your proposal.
explanation: The noun 'objection' is followed by the preposition 'to'.

text: He is senior ____ me in the department.
explanation: Latin comparatives such as senior, junior, superior and inferior take 'to', never 'than'.

text: The hall was crowded ____ people.
explanation: 'Crowded with' is the fixed collocation for a place full of people or things.

text: She apologised ____ her mistake.
explanation: One apologises for a fault and to a person.

text: He is fond ____ classical music.
explanation: The adjective 'fond' is always followed by 'of'.

text: The child is entirely dependent ____ his parents.
explanation: 'Dependent' takes the preposition 'on' before the person or thing relied upon.

text: The prisoners were deprived ____ their basic rights.
explanation: 'Deprive' is followed by 'of' before the thing taken away.

text: The suspect was charged ____ murder.
explanation: A person is charged with an offence, though accused of it.

text: Pakistan came into being ____ 14 August 1947.
explanation: 'On' is used with particular dates and days; 'in' is used with months and years.

text: The class begins ____ eight o'clock every morning.
explanation: 'At' is used with an exact clock time.

text: The rain prevented us ____ going out.
explanation: 'Prevent someone from doing something' is the fixed pattern.

text: He has completely recovered ____ his illness.
explanation: 'Recover' takes 'from' before an illness or setback.

text: A true artist is indifferent ____ criticism.
explanation: The adjective 'indifferent' is followed by 'to'.

text: Each of the boys ____ given a prize.
explanation: 'Each of' is followed by a plural noun but always takes a singular verb.

text: Neither of the answers ____ correct.
explanation: 'Neither of' refers to one of two and therefore takes a singular verb.

text: The news ____ very disturbing.
explanation: 'News' is plural in form but singular in meaning and takes a singular verb.

text: Mathematics ____ my favourite subject.
explanation: Names of subjects ending in -ics take a singular verb.

text: Ten miles ____ a long distance to walk.
explanation: A plural expression of distance, weight or amount treated as one whole takes a singular verb.

text: A number of students ____ absent today.
explanation: 'A number of' means 'many' and therefore takes a plural verb.

text: The number of students in this class ____ fifty.
explanation: 'The number' is a singular noun phrase and takes a singular verb, unlike 'a number of'.

text: Bread and butter ____ a wholesome breakfast.
explanation: Two nouns joined by 'and' that name a single idea or dish take a singular verb.

text: Neither the teacher nor the students ____ present in the hall.
explanation: With 'neither ... nor' the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it, here the plural 'students'.

text: One of my friends ____ a doctor in Multan.
explanation: The subject is 'one', not 'friends', so the verb is singular.

text: The quality of these mangoes ____ not good.
explanation: The verb agrees with the head noun 'quality', not with the noun in the intervening phrase.

text: The cattle ____ grazing in the field.
explanation: 'Cattle' is a collective noun that is always plural in construction.

text: Everybody ____ his own opinion about the matter.
explanation: Indefinite pronouns like everybody, somebody and nobody are singular.

text: Not only the students but also the teacher ____ absent.
explanation: With 'not only ... but also' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, here the singular 'teacher'.

text: Each boy and each girl ____ been given a separate book.
explanation: Singular nouns preceded by 'each' or 'every' and joined by 'and' still take a singular verb.

text: My trousers ____ torn at the knee.
explanation: Nouns naming double garments or instruments, such as trousers and scissors, take a plural verb.

text: Two-thirds of the work ____ been completed.
explanation: With a fraction the verb follows the noun that comes after 'of', and 'work' is uncountable and singular.

text: There ____ many people in the hall.
explanation: In 'there' sentences the verb agrees with the real subject that follows it, here plural 'people'.

text: Slow and steady ____ the race.
explanation: The two adjectives express one idea and are treated as a singular subject.

text: Either of the two roads ____ to the station.
explanation: 'Either of' means one or the other of two and takes a singular verb.

text: Between you and ____, the plan is bound to fail.
explanation: A pronoun after a preposition must be in the objective case, so 'me' is required.

text: Each of the girls did ____ best in the competition.
explanation: 'Each' is singular, and since the reference is to girls the singular possessive 'her' is used.

text: This pen is ____; I bought it yesterday.
explanation: A possessive pronoun standing alone after the verb is 'mine', not the adjective 'my'.

text: He hurt ____ while cutting vegetables.
explanation: When the subject and the object are the same person, the reflexive pronoun is used.

text: Neither of the boys has done ____ homework.
explanation: 'Neither of' is singular, so the singular possessive adjective agrees with it.

text: The dog wagged ____ tail happily.
explanation: 'Its' is the possessive adjective, while 'it's' is the contraction of 'it is'.

text: ____ book is lying on the table?
explanation: 'Whose' is the interrogative possessive form; 'who's' means 'who is'.

text: The man ____ helped me was a complete stranger.
explanation: 'Who' is the relative pronoun used for persons in the subject position.

text: To ____ should I address this letter?
explanation: After a preposition the objective form 'whom' is used.

text: The students submitted ____ assignments before the deadline.
explanation: 'Their' is the possessive adjective before a noun; 'there' shows place and 'they're' means 'they are'.

text: One should keep ____ promises.
explanation: The indefinite pronoun 'one' is referred back to by 'one's'.

text: We enjoyed ____ at the wedding.
explanation: 'Enjoy' used in this sense needs a reflexive object, and the plural reflexive of 'we' is 'ourselves'.

text: Those books on the top shelf are ____.
explanation: 'Theirs' is the possessive pronoun used without a following noun.

text: The house ____ roof is red belongs to my uncle.
explanation: 'Whose' serves as the possessive relative pronoun for things as well as persons.

text: He has ____ money; he cannot even pay his rent.
explanation: 'Little' with an uncountable noun has the negative sense of hardly any, which the second clause confirms.

text: He has ____ friends in this city, so he is never lonely.
explanation: 'A few' has the positive sense of some, which fits a countable noun and the meaning of the sentence.

text: How ____ sugar do you need for the cake?
explanation: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns such as sugar.

text: There are not ____ books on this shelf.
explanation: 'Many' is used with plural countable nouns.

text: He did not give me ____ help at all.
explanation: 'Any' is the form normally used with an uncountable noun in a negative sentence.

text: ____ boy in the class has been given a book.
explanation: 'Every' is used before a singular countable noun taking a singular verb.

text: ____ of the two sisters is a doctor; the other is an engineer.
explanation: The phrase 'the other' shows that exactly one of the two is meant.

text: ____ of these mangoes are ripe.
explanation: Only 'all' takes the plural verb 'are'; 'each' and 'every' require a singular verb.

text: He gave me ____ advice about my career.
explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable, so it takes 'some' and cannot take 'a', 'many' or 'few'.

text: ____ of the three candidates was selected for the post.
explanation: 'None' is used for more than two, while 'neither' and 'either' are restricted to two.

text: He has ____ knowledge of Arabic and can read the text easily.
explanation: 'A little' is the positive form used with an uncountable noun such as knowledge.

text: I do not like ____ of these two shirts.
explanation: After a negative verb 'either' is used for two things; 'neither' would make the sentence doubly negative.

text: There is not ____ milk left in the jug.
explanation: 'Much' is the quantifier used with uncountable nouns in negative sentences.

text: He is a doctor, ____?
explanation: A positive statement takes a negative tag using the same auxiliary and subject.

text: You will come tomorrow, ____?
explanation: The auxiliary 'will' in a positive statement is repeated in the negative tag as 'won't'.

text: Let's go for a walk, ____?
explanation: A sentence beginning with 'Let's' always takes the tag 'shall we'.

text: Open the door, ____?
explanation: An imperative sentence takes the tag 'will you'.

text: She never comes late, ____?
explanation: 'Never' makes the statement negative in meaning, so the tag is positive.

text: I am right, ____?
explanation: The accepted negative tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I', since 'amn't' is not used in standard English.

text: There is no water in the jug, ____?
explanation: 'No' makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive and keeps the introductory 'there'.

text: He has finished his work, ____?
explanation: The auxiliary 'has' of the present perfect is repeated in the negative tag.

text: He used to smoke, ____?
explanation: 'Used to' refers to past habit and takes the auxiliary 'did' in the tag.

text: She can swim across the river, ____?
explanation: The modal 'can' is repeated in the contracted negative tag 'can't she'.

text: What does the idiom 'to bury the hatchet' mean?
explanation: The phrase comes from the Native American custom of burying weapons when hostilities ended, so it means to settle a dispute and become friendly again.

text: What does the idiom 'a wild goose chase' mean?
explanation: A wild goose chase is a pursuit that has no chance of success, because a wild goose can never be caught by chasing it.

text: What does the idiom 'a bolt from the blue' mean?
explanation: It refers to lightning striking out of a clear blue sky, and therefore to something that happens without any warning.

text: What does the idiom 'to smell a rat' mean?
options: To suspect that something is wrong
explanation: The expression describes the sense that something dishonest or deceitful is going on, even before there is proof.

text: What does the idiom 'to bell the cat' mean?
options: To undertake a risky task for the benefit of others
explanation: In the fable the mice agreed that a bell should be tied round the cat's neck, but none dared to do it, so the phrase means taking on a dangerous duty for the common good.

text: What does the idiom 'once in a blue moon' mean?
explanation: A blue moon is an unusual occurrence, so the phrase indicates something that happens extremely seldom.

text: What does the idiom 'to beat about the bush' mean?
options: To avoid coming to the point
explanation: It describes talking round a subject instead of dealing with it directly.

text: What does the idiom 'a white elephant' mean?
options: A possession that is costly to keep and of no use
explanation: The phrase comes from the ruinous expense of keeping a sacred white elephant given as a royal gift, and now means a burdensome and useless asset.

text: What does the idiom 'to let the cat out of the bag' mean?
explanation: It means to reveal information that was meant to be kept hidden.

text: What does the idiom 'to hit the nail on the head' mean?
options: To finish a job in haste
To say exactly the right thing
explanation: It means to describe a situation or state a point with complete accuracy.

text: What does the idiom 'to burn the midnight oil' mean?
options: To work or study late into the night
explanation: Before electricity, working after dark meant burning oil in a lamp, so the phrase means labouring far into the night.

text: What does the idiom 'to be at daggers drawn' mean?
options: To be bitterly hostile to each other
To be on very friendly terms
To be fully armed for battle
explanation: The image of two people with daggers unsheathed conveys open and bitter enmity.

text: What does the expression 'a red-letter day' mean?
explanation: Important feast days were marked in red on old calendars, so the phrase means an especially happy or significant day.

text: What does the idiom 'to add fuel to the fire' mean?
options: To make a bad situation worse
explanation: Adding fuel makes a fire burn more fiercely, so the phrase means aggravating an already difficult quarrel or situation.

text: What does the idiom 'to cry over spilt milk' mean?
options: To regret uselessly what cannot be undone
explanation: Once milk is spilt it cannot be recovered, so the phrase refers to pointless lamenting over a loss already suffered.

text: What does the idiom 'to be in hot water' mean?
options: To be in a great hurry
explanation: The phrase means being in difficulty or facing disgrace because of something one has done.

text: What does the idiom 'to make both ends meet' mean?
explanation: It refers to managing to cover one's expenses with the limited money one earns.

text: What does the idiom 'a snake in the grass' mean?
explanation: It describes a treacherous person who pretends friendship while secretly working against one.

text: What does the idiom 'to pull someone's leg' mean?
explanation: It means to tease a person playfully by telling him something untrue.

text: What does the idiom 'to throw in the towel' mean?
explanation: A boxer's second throws a towel into the ring to stop the contest, so the phrase means giving up the struggle.

text: What does the idiom 'to rest on one's laurels' mean?
options: To be satisfied with past success and stop striving
explanation: Laurel wreaths were given to victors, so resting on them means relying on earlier achievements instead of making fresh effort.

text: What does the idiom 'to show the white feather' mean?
options: To behave in a cowardly manner
explanation: A white feather in a gamecock's tail was taken as a sign of poor breeding, and the phrase came to mean showing cowardice.

text: What does the idiom 'to read between the lines' mean?
explanation: It means grasping what is implied rather than what is actually written or said.

text: What does the idiom 'to be all ears' mean?
explanation: The phrase means being eager and completely attentive to what is being said.

text: What does the expression 'a fair-weather friend' mean?
options: A friend who gives good advice
A friend who deserts one in difficulty
explanation: Such a friend stays only while conditions are pleasant and disappears when trouble comes.

text: What does the expression 'the lion's share' mean?
explanation: In Aesop's fable the lion claims almost everything, so the phrase means much the greater part.

text: What does the idiom 'to break the ice' mean?
options: To break an awkward silence and begin conversation
explanation: It means saying or doing something that relieves the stiffness of a first meeting.

text: What does the idiom 'to keep the wolf from the door' mean?
options: To manage to avoid hunger and poverty
To guard a house at night
explanation: The wolf stands for starvation, so the phrase means earning just enough to survive.

text: What does the idiom 'to burn one's boats' mean?
options: To cut off all means of retreat
explanation: Commanders who burnt their ships after landing left their troops no way back, so the phrase means committing oneself irreversibly.

text: What does the idiom 'to carry coals to Newcastle' mean?
options: To trade at a great profit
To work in a coal mine
explanation: Newcastle was a great coal-producing centre, so taking coal there is a pointless and superfluous act.

text: What does the expression 'Hobson's choice' mean?
options: A choice among many good options
A decision made by drawing lots
explanation: Thomas Hobson let customers take only the horse nearest the stable door, so the phrase means taking what is offered or nothing.

text: What does the idiom 'born with a silver spoon in one's mouth' mean?
explanation: The phrase describes someone who inherits wealth and privilege at birth.

text: What does the expression 'a dark horse' mean?
options: A person whose abilities are unknown until tested
explanation: The term comes from racing, where an unknown horse may unexpectedly win, and is applied to a competitor of hidden strength.

text: What does the idiom 'to have cold feet' mean?
options: To lose one's courage at the last moment
explanation: It describes a sudden loss of nerve just before doing something one had planned.

text: What does the idiom 'to nip in the bud' mean?
options: To stop something at an early stage
explanation: Removing a bud prevents the flower from forming, so the phrase means destroying a trouble before it can develop.

text: What does the idiom 'to pay through the nose' mean?
options: To pay an excessively high price
To refuse to pay a debt
explanation: The phrase means being charged far more for something than it is worth.

text: What does the expression 'crocodile tears' mean?
explanation: The crocodile was said to weep while devouring its prey, so the phrase means pretended sympathy.

text: What does the idiom 'to take the bull by the horns' mean?
explanation: It means confronting a problem directly and courageously instead of avoiding it.

text: What does the expression 'the apple of one's eye' mean?
options: A person who is dearly loved
explanation: The phrase denotes someone cherished above all others.

text: What does the idiom 'to fish in troubled waters' mean?
options: To take advantage of a disturbed situation
explanation: It means seeking personal gain from confusion or conflict among others.

text: What does the idiom 'to eat humble pie' mean?
options: To apologise humbly for a mistake
explanation: It means being forced to admit one was wrong and to submit to humiliation.

text: What does the expression 'a man of straw' mean?
options: A person of no substance or importance
explanation: The phrase describes someone without real worth, resources or influence.

text: What does the expression 'a Herculean task' mean?
options: A task requiring enormous strength or effort
explanation: It alludes to the twelve labours of Hercules and therefore means work of extraordinary difficulty.

text: What does the idiom 'to leave no stone unturned' mean?
options: To destroy everything in one's path
To work in a careless manner
explanation: It means making every conceivable effort to achieve an object.

text: What does the expression 'at the eleventh hour' mean?
explanation: The phrase, drawn from the parable of the labourers, means just before it is too late.

text: What does the idiom 'to steal a march on someone' mean?
options: To gain an advantage over someone secretly
explanation: An army that marched while the enemy slept gained ground unnoticed, so the phrase means getting ahead by quiet forethought.

text: What does the idiom 'to turn over a new leaf' mean?
options: To begin reading a new book
To change one's place of residence
To change one's conduct for the better
To take up a new job
explanation: The leaf is a page, and turning it means starting afresh with improved behaviour.

text: What does the expression 'yeoman's service' mean?
explanation: Yeomen were sturdy and dependable soldiers, so the phrase means loyal and valuable help.

text: What does the expression 'the gift of the gab' mean?
options: The ability to speak fluently and persuasively
explanation: The phrase refers to a natural talent for ready and effective speech.

text: What does the proverb 'A stitch in time saves nine' mean?
options: Nine workers do better than one
explanation: Repairing a small tear at once avoids a much larger repair later, so prompt action saves later labour.

text: What does the proverb 'Make hay while the sun shines' mean?
options: One should work only in fine weather
One should use an opportunity while it lasts
Money should be saved for bad days
explanation: Hay can be dried only in sunshine, so the proverb urges people to act while favourable conditions last.

text: What does the proverb 'Too many cooks spoil the broth' mean?
options: Work is spoiled when too many people interfere
Simple food is the best food
explanation: When too many persons direct a single job the result suffers.

text: What does the proverb 'Barking dogs seldom bite' mean?
options: Those who threaten loudly rarely act
explanation: People who make the loudest threats are usually the least likely to carry them out.

text: What does the proverb 'A rolling stone gathers no moss' mean?
options: A person who never settles down gains nothing
explanation: Someone who keeps changing his place or occupation accumulates neither wealth nor standing.

text: What does the proverb 'Birds of a feather flock together' mean?
options: People of the same character keep company
True friends are difficult to find
explanation: Persons of similar tastes and habits naturally associate with one another.

text: What does the proverb 'Empty vessels make the most noise' mean?
options: Those with least knowledge talk the most
Silence is a mark of weakness
An empty pot is of no use
explanation: Shallow and ignorant people are usually the loudest and most boastful talkers.

text: What does the proverb 'All that glitters is not gold' mean?
options: Gold is a very rare metal
An attractive appearance may be deceptive
explanation: Things that look valuable or splendid on the surface are not always genuinely so.

text: What does the proverb 'A drowning man catches at a straw' mean?
options: Small things are the most important
A person in desperate trouble clutches at the slightest hope
Every child should be taught to swim
Help comes when it is least expected
explanation: In extreme distress a person will try even a remedy that offers almost no chance of success.

text: What does the proverb 'Every cloud has a silver lining' mean?
options: Rain is always followed by sunshine
Every misfortune has some hopeful aspect
Nothing in this world lasts forever
explanation: Even in the worst circumstances there is some ground for hope or comfort.

text: What does the proverb 'Where there is a will there is a way' mean?
options: Firm determination finds a means to succeed
A written will settles all disputes
explanation: A person who is genuinely resolved to do something will discover a method of doing it.

text: The cricket match was ______ because of heavy rain.
explanation: To call off something is to cancel it, which is what happens to a match stopped by rain.

text: He ______ his father in both looks and temper.
explanation: To take after a relative means to resemble that person in appearance or character.

text: We have ______ of sugar and must buy some more.
explanation: To run out of something is to exhaust the whole supply of it.

text: The aircraft is due to ______ at six in the morning.
explanation: An aeroplane takes off when it leaves the ground and begins its flight.

text: Please ______ the fan when you leave the room.
explanation: To turn off an appliance is to stop it by means of a switch.

text: On his doctor's advice he ______ smoking.
explanation: To give up a habit is to abandon it altogether.

text: She ______ her invalid mother for many years.
explanation: To look after a person is to take care of him or her.

text: If you do not know this word, ______ its meaning in the dictionary.
explanation: To look up a word is to find its meaning in a dictionary or reference book.

text: A fire ______ in the factory late at night.
explanation: Fires, wars and epidemics break out, that is, they begin suddenly.

text: His writing is so untidy that I cannot ______ a single word.
explanation: To make out something is to manage to see, read or understand it with difficulty.

text: He ______ the offer of a job in Dubai because the pay was poor.
explanation: To turn down an offer is to refuse or reject it.

text: Students must ______ their assignments before Friday.
explanation: To hand in work is to submit it to the teacher or authority concerned.

text: Our car ______ on the motorway and we had to walk to the next town.
explanation: A vehicle or machine breaks down when it stops working because of a fault.

text: The police are ______ the cause of the accident.
explanation: To look into a matter is to investigate or examine it.

text: His grandfather ______ peacefully in his sleep last winter.
explanation: To pass away is a polite expression meaning to die.

text: The government decided to ______ the outdated law.
explanation: To do away with something is to abolish or get rid of it.

text: The army ______ the rebellion within a week.
explanation: To put down a revolt is to suppress or crush it by force.

text: The meeting has been ______ till next Monday.
explanation: To put off an engagement is to postpone it to a later date.

text: It took the firemen two hours to ______ the blaze.
explanation: To put out a fire is to extinguish it.

text: I cannot ______ his rude behaviour any longer.
explanation: To put up with something is to endure or tolerate it.

text: He ______ a large fortune after the death of his uncle.
explanation: To come into money or property is to receive it as an inheritance.

text: I ______ an old classmate at the railway station yesterday.
explanation: To run into a person is to meet him unexpectedly.

text: The bomb ______ in a crowded market.
explanation: A bomb or firearm goes off when it explodes or is discharged.

text: I ______ meeting you again next month.
explanation: To look forward to something is to await it with pleasure.

text: We should never ______ people who are poor.
explanation: To look down upon someone is to regard him as inferior.

text: The chief guest ______ the prizes to the winners.
explanation: To give away prizes is to distribute or present them formally.

text: She was ______ by her grandmother after her parents died.
explanation: To bring up a child is to rear and educate him or her.

text: The new policy ______ a great change in the economy.
explanation: To bring about something is to cause it to happen.

text: The orders of the court were ______ without delay.
explanation: To carry out an order is to execute or perform it.

text: It took him three months to ______ his illness.
explanation: To get over an illness or shock is to recover from it.

text: He does not ______ his colleagues in the office.
explanation: To get along with people is to live or work with them on friendly terms.

text: The letters PIA ______ Pakistan International Airlines.
explanation: To stand for something is to represent or symbolise it.

text: A true friend ______ you in times of trouble.
explanation: To stand by a person is to support him loyally in difficulty.

text: The present situation ______ immediate action.
explanation: To call for something is to require or demand it.

text: He decided to ______ his expenses in order to save money.
explanation: To cut down expenses is to reduce them.

text: Thieves ______ the house while the family was away.
explanation: To break into a building is to enter it forcibly, usually in order to steal.

text: He did not ______ at the party although he had promised to come.
explanation: To turn up is to arrive or make an appearance.

text: He ______ of the agreement at the last moment.
explanation: To back out of an agreement is to withdraw from a commitment already made.

text: I went to the airport to ______ my friend.
explanation: To see someone off is to go to the station or airport to say goodbye at his departure.

text: The child was ______ by a speeding bus.
explanation: A person is run over when a vehicle knocks him down and passes over him.

text: While cleaning the store room I ______ an old photograph.
explanation: To come across something is to find it by chance.

text: You can ______ me for help whenever you need it.
explanation: To count on someone is to depend or rely on him.

text: He ______ the candles on his birthday cake.
explanation: To blow out a flame is to extinguish it with a puff of breath.

text: He ______ his partner over the division of the profits.
explanation: To fall out with someone is to quarrel and cease to be on good terms.

text: He ______ his friends by breaking his promise.
explanation: To let someone down is to disappoint him by failing to do what was expected.

text: He worked extra hours to ______ the time he had lost.
explanation: To make up for something is to compensate for it.

text: The rumour ______ to be completely false.
explanation: To turn out is to prove to be so in the end.

text: He ______ a new textile factory in Faisalabad.
explanation: To set up a business or institution is to establish it.

text: He could not ______ the other runners and finished last.
explanation: To keep up with others is to move or progress at the same pace as they do.

text: The schools ______ for the summer vacation next week.
explanation: Schools break up when the term ends and the holidays begin.

text: Change into the passive voice: The boy killed the snake.
options: The snake was killed by the boy.
The snake is killed by the boy.
The snake had been killed by the boy.
The snake was being killed by the boy.
explanation: A simple past active verb (killed) becomes 'was/were + past participle' in the passive, so 'killed' becomes 'was killed'.

text: Change into the passive voice: They are building a new bridge.
options: A new bridge is built by them.
A new bridge is being built by them.
A new bridge has been built by them.
A new bridge was being built by them.
explanation: The present continuous active takes the passive form 'is/are being + past participle'.

text: Change into the passive voice: She has finished the work.
options: The work is finished by her.
The work was finished by her.
The work has been finished by her.
The work had been finished by her.
explanation: Present perfect active (has finished) becomes 'has/have been + past participle' in the passive.

text: Change into the passive voice: Post the letter.
options: You are asked the letter posted.
explanation: An imperative sentence is made passive with the pattern 'Let + object + be + past participle'.

text: Change into the passive voice: People say that he is honest.
options: It is said that he is honest.
He is said by people honest.
It was said that he is honest.
That he is honest is saying.
explanation: Sentences beginning 'People say that...' take the impersonal passive 'It is said that...'.

text: Change into the passive voice: Someone stole my bicycle.
options: My bicycle is stolen by someone.
My bicycle has been stolen by someone.
explanation: The past tense verb becomes 'was stolen', and an indefinite agent such as 'someone' is normally dropped in the passive.

text: Change into the passive voice: Who wrote this letter?
options: Whom this letter was written by?
By whom was this letter written?
By whom this letter was written?
explanation: When the interrogative 'who' is the subject, the passive question begins 'By whom' and keeps the auxiliary before the subject.

text: Change into the passive voice: We must obey our elders.
options: Our elders are obeyed by us.
explanation: After a modal such as 'must', the passive is formed with 'be + past participle'.

text: Change into the passive voice: The gardener is watering the plants.
options: The plants are being watered by the gardener.
The plants are watered by the gardener.
The plants were being watered by the gardener.
The plants have been watered by the gardener.
explanation: Present continuous active becomes 'are being watered' in the passive.

text: Change into the passive voice: Has he done his duty?
options: Was his duty done by him?
Has his duty been done by him?
Is his duty done by him?
Had his duty been done by him?
explanation: Present perfect interrogative takes the passive form 'Has + object + been + past participle'.

text: Change into the active voice: The window was broken by the boy.
options: The boy has broken the window.
The boy had broken the window.
explanation: 'Was broken' is simple past passive, so the active form keeps the simple past: 'broke'.

text: Change into the passive voice: Nobody can solve this puzzle.
options: This puzzle is not solved by anybody.
This puzzle could not be solved by anybody.
This puzzle has not been solved by anybody.
This puzzle cannot be solved by anybody.
explanation: A negative subject such as 'nobody' becomes 'not ... by anybody', and the modal 'can' keeps its form with 'be + past participle'.

text: Change into the passive voice: The manager gave him a reward.
options: He was given a reward by the manager.
He was gave a reward by the manager.
A reward gave to him by the manager.
He has been given a reward by the manager.
explanation: With a verb taking two objects, the indirect object may become the passive subject: 'He was given a reward by the manager.'

text: Change into the passive voice: They had completed the project before the deadline.
options: The project was completed before the deadline.
The project had been completed by them before the deadline.
The project has been completed by them before the deadline.
The project was being completed by them before the deadline.
explanation: Past perfect active (had completed) becomes 'had been + past participle' in the passive.

text: Change into the passive voice: I saw him crossing the road.
options: He is seen crossing the road by me.
He was being seen crossing the road by me.
He was seen crossing the road by me.
He had been seen crossing the road by me.
explanation: The simple past 'saw' becomes 'was seen', and the participle 'crossing' is retained unchanged.

text: Change into the passive voice: The teacher will punish the students.
options: The students are punished by the teacher.
The students will punish by the teacher.
The students would be punished by the teacher.
The students will be punished by the teacher.
explanation: The simple future active becomes 'will be + past participle'.

text: Change into the passive voice: We should help the poor.
options: The poor are helped by us.
The poor must have been helped.
explanation: After the modal 'should', the passive requires 'be + past participle', giving 'should be helped'.

text: Change into the passive voice: Open the door.
explanation: The passive of a command uses the structure 'Let + object + be + past participle'.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said, "I am ill."
options: He said that I am ill.
He said that he is ill.
He said that he was ill.
He said that he has been ill.
explanation: After a past reporting verb the present tense shifts back to the past, and the first-person pronoun changes to the third person.

text: Change into indirect speech: She said to me, "I will help you."
options: She said to me that I will help you.
She said me that she will help me.
She told that she would help me.
She told me that she would help me.
explanation: 'Said to me' becomes 'told me', 'will' becomes 'would', and the pronouns shift to 'she' and 'me'.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said, "The earth revolves round the sun."
options: He said that the earth revolves round the sun.
He said that the earth revolved round the sun.
He said that the earth had revolved round the sun.
He said that the earth would revolve round the sun.
explanation: A universal truth keeps its present tense in indirect speech even after a past reporting verb.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Where are you going?"
options: He said to me where was I going.
He asked me where I was going.
He asked me where was I going.
He asked to me that where I was going.
explanation: A reported question keeps the statement word order (subject before verb) and drops the question mark.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said to her, "Do you know the answer?"
options: He asked her that did she know the answer.
He said her if she knows the answer.
He asked her if she knew the answer.
He asked her does she know the answer.
explanation: A yes/no question is reported with 'if' or 'whether', statement word order and a backshifted verb.

text: Change into indirect speech: The teacher said to the boys, "Stand up."
options: The teacher said the boys to stand up.
The teacher said that the boys stood up.
The teacher told to the boys stand up.
The teacher ordered the boys to stand up.
explanation: A command is reported with a verb such as 'ordered' or 'commanded' followed by the to-infinitive.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Please help me."
options: He requested me to help him.
He said me please to help him.
He ordered me that I help him.
He asked me that please help him.
explanation: A polite appeal containing 'please' is reported with 'requested' plus the to-infinitive.

text: Change into indirect speech: She said, "What a beautiful scene it is!"
options: She said that what a beautiful scene it was.
She exclaimed that it was a very beautiful scene.
She said what a beautiful scene it is.
She asked that it was a beautiful scene.
explanation: Exclamatory sentences are reported with 'exclaimed', and 'what a beautiful' becomes 'a very beautiful'.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said, "Alas! I have lost my purse."
options: He said alas that he lost his purse.
He exclaimed with joy that he had lost his purse.
He exclaimed with sorrow that he had lost his purse.
He said that alas he has lost his purse.
explanation: 'Alas' expresses grief, so it is reported as 'exclaimed with sorrow', and the present perfect backshifts to the past perfect.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "I saw her yesterday."
options: He told me that he saw her yesterday.
He said me that he had seen her yesterday.
He told me that he has seen her the previous day.
He told me that he had seen her the previous day.
explanation: The simple past backshifts to the past perfect and 'yesterday' becomes 'the previous day'.

text: Change into indirect speech: She said, "I shall go tomorrow."
options: She said that she would go the next day.
She said that she will go tomorrow.
She said that she would go tomorrow.
She said that she shall go the next day.
explanation: 'Shall/will' becomes 'would' after a past reporting verb, and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said to them, "Do not make a noise."
options: He said them do not make a noise.
He forbade them to make a noise.
He told them that do not make a noise.
He asked them that they do not make a noise.
explanation: A negative command is reported with 'forbade ... to' (or 'told ... not to'), followed by the infinitive.

text: Change into direct speech: He said that he was busy.
explanation: Reversing the backshift restores the present tense and the first-person pronoun inside the quotation marks.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Let us go for a walk."
options: He said me that let us go for a walk.
He told me that we go for a walk.
He asked me that we should go for a walk.
He proposed to me that we should go for a walk.
explanation: 'Let us' expressing a suggestion is reported with 'proposed/suggested that we should'.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said to his friends, "Good morning."
options: He wished his friends good morning.
He said his friends good morning.
He told to his friends that good morning.
He greeted that it was a good morning.
explanation: Greetings are reported with verbs such as 'wished' or 'greeted', without a that-clause.

text: Change into indirect speech: She said to him, "Thank you."
options: She told him that thank you.
She said that she thanks him.
explanation: An expression of gratitude is reported simply with the verb 'thanked'.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said, "How foolish I am!"
options: He said how foolish he was.
He asked how foolish he was.
He exclaimed that he was very foolish.
He said that how foolish he is.
explanation: 'How + adjective' in an exclamation becomes 'very + adjective' in indirect speech, reported with 'exclaimed'.

text: Change into indirect speech: The mother said, "May my son live long!"
options: The mother said that may her son live long.
The mother wished that her son lives long.
The mother ordered that her son should live long.
The mother prayed that her son might live long.
explanation: An optative sentence is reported with 'prayed/wished that', and 'may' becomes 'might'.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said, "I have been waiting for an hour."
options: He said that he had been waiting for an hour.
He said that he has been waiting for an hour.
He said that he was waiting for an hour.
He said that he would be waiting for an hour.
explanation: The present perfect continuous backshifts to the past perfect continuous in indirect speech.

text: Change into indirect speech: He said to me, "Can you lend me your pen?"
options: He asked me that can I lend him my pen.
He asked me if I could lend him my pen.
He said me whether I can lend him my pen.
He requested me can I lend him my pen.
explanation: A yes/no question takes 'if', statement word order, and 'can' backshifts to 'could'.

text: Choose the correct form: If I ___ rich, I would buy a big house.
explanation: The second conditional expresses an unreal present situation and uses the subjunctive 'were' with all subjects.

text: Choose the correct form: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ at home.
explanation: In the first conditional the if-clause takes the present simple and the main clause takes 'will + base verb'.

text: Choose the correct form: If he had studied hard, he ___ the examination.
explanation: The third conditional pairs 'had + past participle' in the if-clause with 'would have + past participle' in the main clause.

text: Choose the correct form: Unless you work hard, you ___ succeed.
explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not', but the main clause still carries the negative outcome: you will not succeed.

text: Choose the correct form: If I ___ him earlier, I would have told him the truth.
explanation: A past unreal condition requires the past perfect 'had met' in the if-clause.

text: Choose the correct form: Had I known the truth, I ___ you.
explanation: 'Had I known' is an inverted third conditional, so the main clause needs 'would have + past participle'.

text: Choose the correct form: I would have helped him if he ___ me.
explanation: The main clause 'would have helped' fixes this as a third conditional, so the if-clause takes 'had asked'.

text: Choose the correct form: If you heat ice, it ___.
explanation: A general scientific fact takes the zero conditional: present simple in both clauses.

text: Choose the correct form: Were he here, he ___ us with the arrangements.
explanation: 'Were he here' is an inverted second conditional, so the main clause takes 'would + base verb'.

text: Choose the correct form: If he had taken my advice, he ___ in trouble now.
explanation: This is a mixed conditional: a past condition with a present result, so the main clause takes 'would not be'.

text: Choose the correct form: If she ___ earlier, she would have met the minister.
explanation: A third conditional if-clause requires the past perfect 'had come'.

text: Choose the correct form: If I get time, I ___ you tomorrow.
explanation: A real future condition uses the present simple in the if-clause and 'will + base verb' in the main clause.

text: Which sentence is parallel in structure?
options: She likes swimming, dancing and to sing.
She likes to swim, dancing and singing.
She likes swimming, dancing and singing.
She likes swim, dance and singing.
explanation: Items joined by 'and' must share the same grammatical form; here all three are gerunds.

text: Which sentence uses the correlative pair correctly?
options: He not only is intelligent but also hardworking.
He is not only intelligent but hardworking also.
He is not only intelligent, but also he hardworking.
He is not only intelligent but also hardworking.
explanation: 'Not only ... but also' must be followed by grammatically matching elements, here two adjectives.

text: Complete with the parallel form: She is responsible for hiring the staff, training them and ___ their performance.
explanation: The first two items are gerunds ('hiring', 'training'), so the third must also be a gerund.

text: Complete with the parallel form: My duties include answering the phone, greeting visitors and ___ the mail.
explanation: The list consists of gerunds, so 'sorting' preserves parallel structure.

text: Complete with the parallel form: The manager wants his team to work quickly, accurately and ___.
explanation: The series consists of adverbs, so the third item must also be an adverb.

text: Complete with the parallel form: The post requires patience, diligence and ___.
explanation: The first two items are abstract nouns, so the third must be the noun 'honesty'.

text: Complete correctly: He prefers reading books to ___ television.
explanation: After 'prefer ... to', both compared activities must be gerunds: 'reading ... to watching'.

text: Complete with the parallel form: The committee decided to cut costs, to raise prices and ___ the staff.
explanation: The series uses full infinitives, so the third item must also be 'to + base verb'.

text: Complete with the parallel form: He came to the office, signed the register and ___ his seat.
explanation: The three verbs share one subject and must all be in the simple past.

text: Complete the sentence so that the opening phrase is not dangling: Walking down the street, ___
options: I saw the trees in full bloom.
the trees looked beautiful to me.
the trees in full bloom were seen.
explanation: The introductory participle must modify the subject that follows; only 'I' can be walking down the street.

text: Complete the sentence so that the opening phrase is not dangling: Having finished the work, ___
options: the television was switched on by him.
the television was on all evening.
explanation: The person who finished the work must be the subject of the main clause, so 'he' must follow the participial phrase.

text: Which sentence states clearly that the number of mangoes eaten was two and no more?
explanation: 'Only' must stand immediately before the word it limits, so it belongs before 'two mangoes'.

text: Complete the sentence so that the opening phrase is not dangling: To improve his health, ___
options: a gym membership was bought by him.
explanation: An infinitive of purpose must attach to the person who has the purpose, so 'he' must be the subject.

text: Complete the sentence so that the opening phrase is not dangling: Running to catch the bus, ___
options: my bag fell on the road.
explanation: Only a person can run to catch a bus, so the main clause must begin with 'I'.

text: Which sentence makes clear that the man, not the police, was wearing a mask?
options: The man was arrested by the police wearing a mask.
The man wearing a mask was arrested by the police.
Wearing a mask, the police arrested the man.
The man was wearing a mask arrested by the police.
explanation: A modifying phrase should sit next to the noun it describes, so 'wearing a mask' must follow 'the man'.

text: Which version corrects the dangling modifier in 'At the age of five, my mother enrolled me in school'?
options: At five years of age, my mother enrolled me in school.
My mother, at the age of five, enrolled me in school.
When I was five, my mother enrolled me in school.
At the age of five, school was where my mother enrolled me.
explanation: The original wrongly makes the mother five years old; replacing the phrase with a clause naming 'I' removes the error.

text: Complete the sentence so that the opening phrase is not dangling: After reading the original study, ___
options: there was little to convince anyone.
explanation: The reader must be the subject of the main clause, otherwise the article appears to have read the study.

text: Which sentence makes clear that the sandwiches, not the children, were on paper plates?
options: She served sandwiches to the children on paper plates.
She served the children sandwiches on paper plates.
On paper plates she served the children sandwiches.
She served the children on paper plates sandwiches.
explanation: Placing 'sandwiches' immediately before 'on paper plates' attaches the phrase to the food rather than to the children.

text: Which is the correct possessive form for books belonging to children?
explanation: 'Children' is already an irregular plural, so the possessive adds apostrophe + s.

text: Choose the correct word: The dog wagged ___ tail.
explanation: 'Its' is the possessive determiner; 'it's' is the contraction of 'it is'.

text: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
options: I have a meeting at noon; therefore, I cannot join you.
I have a meeting at noon, therefore I cannot join you.
I have a meeting at noon therefore, I cannot join you.
I have a meeting at noon: therefore I cannot join you.
explanation: Two independent clauses linked by the conjunctive adverb 'therefore' require a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

text: The speaker has only one brother. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: My brother who lives in Lahore is a doctor.
My brother, who lives in Lahore, is a doctor.
My brother, who lives in Lahore is a doctor.
My brother who lives in Lahore, is a doctor.
explanation: A non-defining relative clause adds extra information and must be enclosed by a pair of commas.

text: Which sentence uses quotation marks and punctuation correctly?
options: He said, I am going home.
explanation: A comma introduces the quotation, the first word is capitalised, and the full stop falls inside the closing quotation marks.

text: Which sentence punctuates the introduction of the list correctly?
options: She bought three things, bread, milk and eggs.
She bought three things; bread, milk and eggs.
She bought three things - bread; milk; and eggs.
She bought three things: bread, milk and eggs.
explanation: A colon introduces a list that follows a complete independent clause.

text: Choose the correct word: ___ book is lying on the table?
explanation: 'Whose' is the possessive interrogative; 'who's' means 'who is'.

text: Which sentence is punctuated to show that the speaker is addressing Grandma?
explanation: A comma must separate a noun of address from the rest of the sentence.

text: Which sentence is correctly hyphenated?
options: He is a well known writer.
explanation: A compound adjective placed before the noun it modifies takes a hyphen.

text: Which sentence avoids a comma splice?
options: It was getting late, we went home.
It was getting late we went home.
It was getting late, we, went home.
It was getting late, so we went home.
explanation: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone; a coordinating conjunction such as 'so' is needed.

text: Choose the correct verb: Neither of the boys ___ present in the class.
explanation: 'Neither' used as a pronoun is singular and takes a singular verb.

text: Choose the correct verb: The quality of the mangoes ___ not good.
explanation: The subject is the singular noun 'quality'; the prepositional phrase 'of the mangoes' does not change the number.

text: Choose the correct verb: Each of the students ___ been given a book.
explanation: 'Each' is always singular and takes a singular verb regardless of the plural noun that follows.

text: Choose the correct verb: Ten miles ___ a long distance to walk.
explanation: A plural expression of distance, weight or money treated as a single unit takes a singular verb.

text: Choose the correct verb: The news ___ very encouraging.
explanation: 'News' is an uncountable noun that is singular in form and meaning despite the final -s.

text: Choose the correct verb: Mathematics ___ my favourite subject.
explanation: Names of subjects ending in -ics take a singular verb.

text: Choose the correct verb: One of my friends ___ a doctor in Karachi.
explanation: The subject is 'one', which is singular; 'of my friends' merely limits it.

text: Choose the correct verb: Neither he nor his brothers ___ coming to the party.
explanation: With 'neither ... nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, which here is the plural 'brothers'.

text: Choose the correct verb: A number of students ___ absent today.
explanation: 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb, unlike 'the number of', which is singular.

text: Choose the correct verb: Bread and butter ___ my usual breakfast.
explanation: Two nouns naming one combined item take a singular verb.

text: Choose the correct verb: Politics ___ not an easy profession.
explanation: 'Politics' as a field of activity is singular and takes a singular verb.

text: Choose the correct verb: The scissors on the table ___ very sharp.
explanation: Nouns naming instruments made of two parts, such as scissors, are always plural in construction.

text: Choose the correct word: He has been living in this house ___ 2010.
explanation: 'Since' is used with a point in time, while 'for' is used with a length of time.

text: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
explanation: A finished time expression such as 'yesterday' requires the simple past, not the present perfect.

text: Choose the correct form: He said that he ___ come the next day.
explanation: After a past reporting verb, 'will' changes to 'would' under the sequence of tenses.

text: Choose the correct word: Hardly had I reached the station ___ the train left.
explanation: 'Hardly' is followed by 'when'; only 'no sooner' takes 'than'.

text: Choose the correct word: No sooner did he see the police ___ he ran away.
explanation: 'No sooner' is a comparative form and is always followed by 'than'.

text: Choose the correct word: It is three years ___ he left the country.
explanation: The pattern 'It is + period of time + since + past tense' expresses how long ago something happened.

text: Choose the correct word: He is senior ___ me by two years.
explanation: Latin comparatives such as senior, junior, superior and inferior take 'to', never 'than'.

text: Choose the correct word: He prefers tea ___ coffee.
explanation: The verb 'prefer' is followed by 'to' when two things are compared.

text: Choose the correct completion: We shall discuss ___ at tomorrow's meeting.
explanation: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb and takes a direct object without any preposition.

text: Which sentence is free from redundancy?
options: He returned back home late at night.
He repeated the same thing again.
He returned home late at night.
He reverted back to his old habits.
explanation: 'Return' already contains the idea of 'back', so adding 'back' is redundant.

text: Choose the correct word: She could not cope ___ the pressure of work.
explanation: The verb 'cope' is always followed by the preposition 'with'.

text: Choose the correct word: His opinion is quite different ___ mine.
explanation: 'Different' is standardly followed by 'from' in formal written English.

text: Choose the correct word: She is married ___ a civil servant.
explanation: A person is 'married to' another person; 'married with' is incorrect.

text: Choose the correct completion: The committee ___ ten members.
explanation: 'Comprise' means 'consist of' and is used without a preposition.

text: Choose the correct word: This matter must remain a secret between you and ___.
explanation: A pronoun following a preposition must be in the objective case, so 'me' is required.

text: Which sentence uses the comparative degree correctly?
options: He is more intelligent than his brother.
He is more cleverer than his brother.
He is most intelligent than his brother.
He is intelligenter than his brother.
explanation: A comparative is formed either with '-er' or with 'more', never with both, and three-syllable adjectives take 'more'.

text: Choose the correct word: He is the ___ of the two brothers.
explanation: When only two persons are compared, the comparative degree 'elder' is used, not the superlative.

text: Choose the correct verb: Every boy and girl of the school ___ given a prize.
explanation: Nouns joined by 'and' but preceded by 'every' or 'each' are treated as singular.

text: Choose the correct completion: He is not only a poet ___ a novelist of repute.
explanation: 'Not only' pairs exclusively with 'but also' as a correlative conjunction.

text: Choose the correct completion: Neither the principal ___ the teachers were present at the function.
explanation: 'Neither' is always followed by 'nor' in a correlative pair.

text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: The number of students / in the class / are increasing / every year.
explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb, so it should read 'is increasing'.

text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: One of my friend / is coming / to my house / tomorrow.
explanation: 'One of' must be followed by a plural noun, so the phrase should be 'one of my friends'.

text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: He is / more cleverer / than / his brother.
explanation: A double comparative is wrong; the correct form is simply 'cleverer'.

text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: The boy who / was standing / near the gate / have gone away.
explanation: The singular subject 'the boy' requires 'has gone away'.

text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: She is junior / than me / by two years / in service.
explanation: 'Junior' takes the preposition 'to', so the phrase should be 'junior to me'.

text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: The furnitures / in the new office / were bought / last month.
explanation: 'Furniture' is an uncountable noun and has no plural form.

text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: She has a lot of / informations / about the new policy / of the government.
explanation: 'Information' is uncountable and is never used in the plural.

text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: I am looking forward / to meet you / at the conference / next week.
explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition and must be followed by a gerund: 'to meeting you'.

text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: We discussed / the whole matter / but could not / arrive to a conclusion.
explanation: The idiom is 'arrive at a conclusion', not 'arrive to'.

text: Identify the part of the sentence that contains an error: The manager, / along with his assistants, / were present / at the meeting.
explanation: A phrase introduced by 'along with' does not change the number of the subject, so the verb must be 'was present'.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'obfuscate'.
explanation: To obfuscate is to make something deliberately unclear or hard to understand, i.e. to obscure it.

text: A 'laconic' reply is one that is:
explanation: Laconic describes speech or writing that uses very few words.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'ephemeral'.
explanation: Ephemeral means short-lived or fleeting, lasting only for a brief period.

text: An 'intransigent' negotiator is one who is:
explanation: Intransigent means unwilling to change one's position or reach a compromise.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'ubiquitous'.
explanation: Ubiquitous means appearing or existing everywhere at the same time.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'perfidious'.
explanation: Perfidious describes someone who betrays trust; its noun form is perfidy, meaning treachery.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'garrulous'.
explanation: Garrulous describes a person who talks too much, especially about trivial matters.

text: A 'recalcitrant' student is:
explanation: Recalcitrant means resisting authority or discipline in a stubborn, defiant way.

text: A 'sycophant' is best described as:
explanation: A sycophant flatters powerful people insincerely in order to gain advantage.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'nefarious'.
explanation: Nefarious describes acts that are criminal or extremely wicked.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'truculent'.
explanation: Truculent means eager to argue or fight; it has no connection with truth despite the spelling.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'pellucid'.
explanation: Pellucid means transparently clear, whether of water, glass or an explanation.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'munificent'.
explanation: Munificent describes lavish generosity, especially in giving; it is unrelated to 'magnificent'.

text: A 'quixotic' scheme is one that is:
explanation: Quixotic, from Cervantes' Don Quixote, describes hopelessly idealistic plans that ignore practical reality.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'inchoate'.
explanation: Inchoate describes something only recently begun and therefore still rudimentary.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'lugubrious'.
explanation: Lugubrious means looking or sounding sad and dismal, often exaggeratedly so.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'obdurate'.
explanation: Obdurate means hardened against persuasion or pity, that is, stubbornly unyielding.

text: A person described as 'sanguine' about the future is:
explanation: Sanguine means cheerfully confident and hopeful about what is to come.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'effrontery'.
explanation: Effrontery is insolent or impudent behaviour shown without any sense of shame.

text: A 'vituperative' speech is one that is:
explanation: Vituperative language is harsh, bitter and abusive in its criticism.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'fastidious'.
explanation: Fastidious means very attentive to detail and hard to please about cleanliness or accuracy.

text: An 'apocryphal' story is one that is:
explanation: Apocryphal describes a widely circulated account that is probably not genuine or true.

text: To 'prevaricate' is to:
options: Speak evasively to avoid the truth
explanation: To prevaricate is to speak or act in an evasive way in order to avoid telling the truth.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'redolent'.
explanation: Redolent means strongly smelling of something, and by extension strongly suggestive of it.

text: An 'insouciant' manner is one that is:
explanation: Insouciant means showing a relaxed lack of concern or anxiety.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'puerile'.
explanation: Puerile means silly and immature, characteristic of a child rather than an adult.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'cupidity'.
explanation: Cupidity is an excessive desire for money or possessions, not for love.

text: A 'salubrious' climate is one that is:
explanation: Salubrious means health-giving or wholesome, especially of air, climate or surroundings.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'impecunious'.
explanation: Impecunious means habitually short of money, that is, penniless.

text: An 'abstruse' argument is one that is:
explanation: Abstruse means obscure and hard to comprehend without specialised knowledge.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'mendacious'.
explanation: Mendacious means untruthful; the corresponding noun is mendacity.

text: To 'enervate' someone is to:
explanation: Enervate means to weaken or exhaust, despite sounding as though it should mean energise.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'ineluctable'.
explanation: Ineluctable describes something that cannot be resisted or escaped.

text: When attitudes 'ossify', they:
explanation: To ossify is literally to turn into bone, and figuratively to become fixed and inflexible.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'perspicacious'.
explanation: Perspicacious describes a person with keen insight and quick understanding.

text: To 'ameliorate' a situation is to:
explanation: Ameliorate means to improve or make something bad more tolerable.

text: An 'obsequious' assistant is one who is:
explanation: Obsequious means attentive to an excessive, servile degree in order to win favour.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'anodyne'.
explanation: An anodyne is something that relieves pain, and as an adjective it means bland and unlikely to offend.

text: Knowledge described as 'esoteric' is:
options: Understood by only a small group
explanation: Esoteric knowledge is intended for or understood by only a few people with special interest or training.

text: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'pusillanimous'.
explanation: Pusillanimous means showing a lack of courage or determination.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'prodigal'.
explanation: Prodigal means recklessly extravagant with money, so its opposite is thrifty.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'taciturn'.
explanation: Taciturn means saying very little, so its opposite is loquacious, meaning talkative.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'exacerbate'.
explanation: Exacerbate means to make a problem worse; alleviate means to make it less severe.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'nadir'.
explanation: The nadir is the lowest point of something; the zenith is the highest.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'ostentatious'.
explanation: Ostentatious means designed to impress by conspicuous display, the opposite of unpretentious.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'voluble'.
explanation: Voluble means speaking easily and at length; reticent means unwilling to speak.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'ratify'.
explanation: To ratify is to give formal consent to an agreement; to annul is to declare it invalid.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'diffident'.
explanation: Diffident means shy and lacking self-confidence, so its opposite is self-assured.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'amalgamate'.
explanation: Amalgamate means to merge two or more things into one, the opposite of separating them.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'extol'.
explanation: To extol is to praise highly; to denigrate is to belittle or disparage.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'culpable'.
explanation: Culpable means deserving blame, so its opposite is blameless.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'pristine'.
explanation: Pristine means clean and untouched; sullied means soiled or spoiled.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'magnanimous'.
explanation: Magnanimous means generous and forgiving towards a rival, the opposite of vindictive.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'ebullient'.
explanation: Ebullient means overflowing with enthusiasm; despondent means dejected and low in spirits.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'innocuous'.
explanation: Innocuous means causing no injury or offence, so its opposite is harmful.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'alacrity'.
explanation: Alacrity is brisk and cheerful readiness, the opposite of reluctance.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'perfunctory'.
explanation: A perfunctory action is done as a routine duty without care, so its opposite is thorough.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'cacophony'.
explanation: Cacophony is a harsh, discordant mixture of sounds; euphony is pleasing, harmonious sound.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'antipathy'.
explanation: Antipathy is a deep-seated dislike; affinity is a natural liking or attraction.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'laud'.
explanation: To laud is to praise; to censure is to criticise severely and formally.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'placate'.
explanation: To placate is to calm someone's anger; to provoke is to arouse it.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'erudite'.
explanation: Erudite means having or showing great scholarly learning, so its opposite is ignorant.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'sporadic'.
explanation: Sporadic means occurring at irregular intervals; incessant means never ceasing.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'callous'.
explanation: Callous means insensitive to the suffering of others, the opposite of compassionate.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'vindicate'.
explanation: To vindicate is to clear someone of blame; to incriminate is to show them to be guilty.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'abstemious'.
explanation: Abstemious means sparing in eating and drinking, so its opposite is self-indulgent.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'rescind'.
explanation: To rescind is to cancel a law or order; to enact is to bring one into force.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'docile'.
explanation: Docile means easily managed or taught; intractable means stubbornly difficult to control.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'paucity'.
explanation: Paucity means a shortage or smallness of supply, so its opposite is abundance.

text: Choose the word most nearly opposite in meaning to 'clandestine'.
explanation: Clandestine means kept secret because it is illicit; overt means done openly.

text: One word for a person who speaks many languages:
explanation: A polyglot knows and is able to use several languages.

text: One word for a person who hates mankind:
explanation: A misanthrope dislikes humankind in general, while a misogynist dislikes women in particular.

text: Government by the wealthy is called:
explanation: Plutocracy is rule by the rich, from the Greek 'ploutos' meaning wealth.

text: A speech delivered without previous preparation is called:
explanation: An extempore speech is made on the spur of the moment without prior preparation.

text: A poem of mourning for the dead is called:
explanation: An elegy is a poem of serious reflection, typically a lament for someone who has died.

text: Words inscribed on a tombstone are called:
explanation: An epitaph is the inscription written on a tomb in memory of the person buried there.

text: An abnormal fear of enclosed spaces is called:
explanation: Claustrophobia is the fear of confined or enclosed spaces.

text: One word for a person who remains unaffected by pleasure or pain:
explanation: A stoic endures hardship and pleasure alike without showing feeling or complaint.

text: One word for a person who holds that nothing can be known about the existence of God:
explanation: An agnostic believes that the existence of God can neither be proved nor disproved, unlike an atheist who denies it.

text: A supposed remedy for all diseases is called:
explanation: A panacea is a single cure claimed to work for every disease or difficulty.

text: The killing of a king is called:
explanation: Regicide is the killing of a king, from the Latin 'rex' meaning king.

text: One word for a person who abandons his religious faith:
explanation: An apostate is one who renounces a religious or political belief he formerly held.

text: One word for a raw beginner in a skill or trade:
explanation: A tyro is a novice or beginner, the opposite of an expert such as a maestro or virtuoso.

text: The study of the origin and history of words is called:
explanation: Etymology traces the derivation and historical development of words; entomology is the study of insects.

text: One word for a person who cannot be reformed or corrected:
explanation: Incorrigible describes a person whose bad habits cannot be corrected or reformed.

text: One word for a person who withdraws from society and lives alone:
explanation: A recluse lives in solitude, avoiding contact with other people.

text: One word for a person who never drinks alcohol:
explanation: A teetotaller is someone who abstains completely from alcoholic drink.

text: Favouritism shown by those in power to their own relatives is called:
explanation: Nepotism is the granting of jobs or privileges to relatives regardless of merit.

text: One word for a person who falsely claims to have special knowledge or skill:
explanation: A charlatan is an impostor who pretends to expertise he does not possess.

text: A mild or indirect expression substituted for a harsh or blunt one is called:
explanation: A euphemism softens an unpleasant idea, as in saying 'passed away' for 'died'.

text: One word for a person who is too ready to believe things:
explanation: Credulous describes a person willing to believe without proof; credible describes a claim that is believable.

text: One word for a person who attacks cherished beliefs and established institutions:
explanation: An iconoclast attacks or ridicules settled beliefs and revered institutions.

text: One word for a person of wide and varied learning:
explanation: A polymath has expert knowledge across many different subjects.

text: A scene of wild and noisy disorder is called:
explanation: Pandemonium, a word coined by Milton, means utter uproar and confusion.

text: One word for a person who is unable to pay his debts:
explanation: An insolvent person cannot meet his financial obligations as they fall due.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of SCALPEL : SURGEON.
explanation: A scalpel is the cutting tool used by a surgeon just as a chisel is the cutting tool used by a sculptor.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of PARSIMONIOUS : MISER.
explanation: Parsimonious names the defining quality of a miser, as garrulous names the defining quality of a chatterbox.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of BIBLIOPHILE : BOOKS.
explanation: A bibliophile is a lover and collector of books, as a philatelist is a collector of stamps.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of LEXICOGRAPHER : DICTIONARY.
explanation: A lexicographer compiles dictionaries as a cartographer draws maps; both pairs are maker and product.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of EMOLLIENT : SOOTHE.
explanation: An emollient is applied in order to soothe, as a stimulant is taken in order to excite.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of PENURY : WEALTH.
explanation: Penury is an extreme lack of wealth, just as famine is an extreme lack of food.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of SONNET : POEM.
explanation: A sonnet is a particular kind of poem, as a waltz is a particular kind of dance.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of APIARY : BEES.
explanation: An apiary is a place where bees are kept, as an aviary is an enclosure where birds are kept.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of GLUTTON : FOOD.
explanation: A glutton consumes food to excess, as a drunkard consumes liquor to excess.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of AUDACIOUS : TIMID.
explanation: Audacious and timid are opposites, and of the choices only prudent and reckless are opposites.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of ORNITHOLOGY : BIRDS.
explanation: Ornithology is the study of birds, as entomology is the study of insects.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of ARCHIPELAGO : ISLANDS.
explanation: An archipelago is a group of islands, as a constellation is a group of stars.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of ANTIDOTE : POISON.
explanation: An antidote counteracts a poison, as a remedy counteracts an ailment.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of PLETHORA : SCARCITY.
explanation: A plethora is an over-supply and scarcity is a shortage, an opposition matched only by surplus and deficit.

text: Choose the pair whose relationship is most like that of PROFLIGATE : THRIFT.
explanation: A profligate person lacks thrift, as a miserly person lacks generosity; the other pairs show possession, not absence.
